subtype: Approach: planning for the holidays with a neighbour [Thinking]
passage: Note from Sabina, next-door neighbour. Hansa knocked on our door on Saturday with a list. Her family leaves for a week on Monday, and she asked whether I could water her pots each morning. She had already moved all six pots together beside our shared wall. "So you only walk a few steps," she explained. On a card she had written how much water each pot gets. When I asked why she was planning so early, she said, "A week is a long time for a thirsty plant." I said yes, and pinned the card inside my kitchen door. - Sabina

qa.q: How many pots did Hansa move together?
qa.a: Hansa moved all six pots together beside the shared wall.

qa.q: What might Hansa have been worried about before the trip?
qa.a: Hansa was probably worried about the plants going thirsty while the family is away, which is why she planned early.

qa.q: What else could Hansa do to support the neighbour, and why?
qa.a: Hansa could leave a family phone number and a watering can in an easy spot, so the neighbour can ask if something looks wrong.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Hansa's request?
qa.a: Sabina finds it well prepared and easy to say yes to, since the pots are grouped and the card explains the watering.

grounding: A girl who knows her family will be away for a week arranges for a neighbour to water the pots and groups them together.

subtype: Approach: making a feeding and cleaning schedule [Action]
passage: In the waiting room of the animal clinic, Ujjwal held his new puppy in his lap while the nurse, Binita, handed him a blank card. "Tell me a day with him," she said. Ujjwal wrote: 7 a.m., food. After school, walk. 6 p.m., food. Bedtime, check the water bowl. His mother nodded at each line. At home he pinned the card beside the front door with a red drawing pin. By the third evening his sister was reading it aloud before feeding time, and Ujjwal never had to remind anyone.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal pin the card?
qa.a: He pinned the card beside the front door.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling about the puppy as he wrote the card?
qa.a: Excited and committed, since he wrote out every part of a day with the puppy.

qa.q: What could the family do if a task on the card gets missed, and why?
qa.a: They could add tick boxes or take turns by day, so everyone can see what has been done.

qa.q: How might Binita see the card Ujjwal wrote?
qa.a: Binita probably sees a good start, since a written routine helps a new owner keep the puppy's care regular.

grounding: A boy with a new puppy writes a feeding, walking and water-check schedule and pins it where the family follows it.

subtype: Approach: observing the animal's behaviour to understand needs [Thinking]
passage: Irawati's cat, Golu, usually sprang out from under the sofa at the sound of the food bowl. Today he stayed under it, eyes half shut. The morning's bowl was still full. "He's sulking because I came home late," said her brother Shankar. Irawati crouched and looked for longer. "Sulking cats still eat." Hiding and not eating, both at once, was not what Golu usually did. "Amma, please call the vet." Her mother frowned, peered under the sofa and reached for the phone. The vet said to bring Golu in that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Irawati notice about the food bowl?
qa.a: The morning's bowl was still full.

qa.q: What was Irawati thinking as she crouched by the sofa?
qa.a: She was worried that something was wrong, since sulking cats still eat, so she did not accept Shankar's guess.

qa.q: What could Irawati do while waiting for the vet, and why?
qa.a: She could write down what she has seen, such as hiding and the full bowl, so she can tell the vet clearly.

qa.q: Why might Shankar think Golu is sulking?
qa.a: Shankar came home late, so he links the cat's mood to that, and may not have noticed the full bowl.

grounding: A girl reads a cat's hiding and not eating as a sign something may be wrong, and asks her mother to call the vet.

subtype: Approach: enthusiasm early and neglect later [Pitfall]
passage: At the school pet club, Vishal proudly announced that his rabbit, Snow, was thriving. Jomon Sir asked, "What does Snow need at six every evening?" Vishal opened his mouth and shut it. Three weeks ago he had begged for the rabbit and promised to do everything, and for two weeks he had. Then the football league began and the newness faded. Lately Mummy fed Snow and Papa cleaned the cage while he pretended not to notice. His cheeks grew warm. "Well... mostly Mummy now." Jomon Sir nodded slowly and let the silence sit.

qa.q: How long did Vishal care for the rabbit eagerly?
qa.a: He cared for the rabbit eagerly for two weeks.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when Jomon Sir asked what Snow needs at six?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a little guilty, since his cheeks grew warm and he could not answer.

qa.q: What could Vishal do to start again, and why?
qa.a: He could make a small schedule and take back one job each day, starting with feeding, so caring becomes a habit rather than a burst.

qa.q: How might Vishal's parents feel about doing the rabbit's care?
qa.a: They are probably tired and a bit concerned, since they took over the feeding and cleaning while hoping Vishal would learn.

grounding: A child begs for a rabbit and cares for it eagerly for two weeks, until the newness fades and the parents take over.

subtype: Approach: asking an expert about the right food [Action]
passage: Yesterday I took my puppy for her first check. I asked Dr Tanvir, "What should I feed her?" Dr Tanvir said puppy food is best, that anything with chocolate or leftover curry is not safe for her, and to ask before adding anything new. At home I sat with Mama and Papa and we wrote a meal plan on a card, with the two unsafe foods in red. Then I stuck it inside the kitchen cupboard. My puppy sniffed the card, which made everyone laugh. I have never seen Papa read a card so seriously. - Amandeep

qa.q: Which foods did the vet say are not safe for the puppy?
qa.a: The vet said chocolate and leftover curry are not safe for the puppy.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the puppy sniffed the card?
qa.a: Happy and amused, sharing a laugh with the family.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep ask the vet next time, and why?
qa.a: Amandeep could ask what changes as the puppy grows, so the meal plan can be updated with the vet's help.

qa.q: How might Mama and Papa see Amandeep's meal plan?
qa.a: They are probably pleased that Amandeep asked an expert first, and they join in the plan seriously.

grounding: A child asks the vet what to feed a puppy, learns that chocolate and spicy leftovers are unsafe, and makes a meal plan with the parents.

subtype: Approach: learning from a mistake with the pet [Revision]
passage: I put the fish tank on the windowsill because it looked pretty in the sun. By afternoon the little orange fish were gulping near the top, and when I touched the water it felt like tea. My heart thumped. "Madhuri Didi, come quick!" Didi said, "Move it away from the window," and helped me carry it to the shaded corner by the bookshelf. I felt awful. That night I taped a thermometer to the glass and added "temperature" to my daily checks, next to feeding and water level. - Nandini

qa.q: Where did Nandini move the tank?
qa.a: Nandini moved it to the shaded corner by the bookshelf.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel about the mistake?
qa.a: Awful and worried, since Nandini's heart thumped and the fish were gulping near the top.

qa.q: What could Nandini do so the mistake is not repeated, and why?
qa.a: Nandini could keep the tank in the shade for good and check the temperature at the same time every day, so a change is noticed early.

qa.q: How might Madhuri Didi see the situation?
qa.a: Madhuri Didi stays calm and acts fast, telling Nandini to move the tank and helping carry it.

grounding: A girl leaves the fish tank in direct sun, finds the water too warm, moves it to shade and adds a thermometer check.

subtype: Approach: training through small rewards and repetition [Action]
passage: At the community centre's Saturday pet class, Arnab held a treat above his dog's nose and said, "Sit." The dog sat, and Arnab handed over a tiny treat at once. Again, five times. "Only a few minutes at a time," said the instructor, Nirmala Ma'am. "Stop while it's still fun." Arnab did that every day for a week. Only when the dog sat every single time did he take one step back before saying the word. By the next Saturday he could stand three steps away and the dog still sat, tail thumping against the floor.

qa.q: What did Arnab give the dog each time it sat?
qa.a: He gave the dog a tiny treat at once.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when the dog sat from three steps away?
qa.a: Proud and happy, since the daily practice had worked.

qa.q: What could Arnab do if the dog stops obeying, and why?
qa.a: He could go back to an easier step for a while, so the dog earns treats again and the habit rebuilds.

qa.q: How does Nirmala Ma'am see Arnab's method?
qa.a: Nirmala Ma'am sees a patient learner following her advice about short sessions and small steps.

grounding: A boy teaches his dog to sit with small rewards and daily repetition, adding difficulty only after each success.

subtype: Approach: thinking of the pet as a family member with rights [Thinking]
passage: Behind the village school, Tushar called across the field, "One more game, Aadhya! The sun is still up." Aadhya looked at the long shadows. She thought of Moti, her dog, lying by the gate since noon with his chin on his paws. "Food and water is not everything," she thought. "He needs a walk and someone to sit with him. He is not a stone." "I can't stay," she called back. "Moti is waiting." Tushar shrugged, a little disappointed. She ran home, and Moti jumped up so fast that he knocked his bowl over.

qa.q: Where had Moti been lying since noon?
qa.a: Moti had been lying by the gate.

qa.q: What was Aadhya thinking as she looked at the long shadows?
qa.a: She was concerned that Moti was lonely and needed her company, not only food.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do so that both the game and Moti are looked after, and why?
qa.a: She could bring Moti to the field or fix a walk right after the game, so her friends and her dog both get time.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel when Aadhya leaves?
qa.a: Tushar is a little disappointed, as his shrug shows, since he wanted one more game.

grounding: A girl reasons that her dog needs walks and company as well as food, and tells her friends she must go home.

subtype: Approach: forcing a frightened animal to play [Pitfall]
passage: At the animal shelter's Sunday visit, Divyansh spotted a grey kitten crouching at the back of the pen. He picked it up and hugged it against his chest. Its ears flattened and its tail lashed, but he did not notice. He put it down, then picked it up again. "She's so soft!" The kitten's claws raked across his wrist. "Ow!" He dropped it. Trisha, the volunteer, came over with a wet cloth. "Ears back, tail flicking. She was telling you she needed space. Look at her now." The kitten sat under a shelf, watching. Divyansh looked at the red scratches, then at the kitten, and felt bad for both.

qa.q: What happened when Divyansh kept picking up the kitten?
qa.a: The kitten's claws raked across his wrist.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling at the end of the scene?
qa.a: Sorry and a little upset, since he felt bad for both himself and the kitten.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do instead of picking the kitten up, and why?
qa.a: He could sit quietly and let the kitten come to him, since a frightened animal is easier to befriend when it can choose.

qa.q: What might it be like for the kitten when it is picked up again and again?
qa.a: The kitten was probably frightened and wanted space, as its flattened ears and lashing tail suggest.

grounding: A boy keeps picking up a nervous kitten to cuddle it, ignores its signals and gets scratched.

subtype: Approach: planning for the pet during travel [Thinking]
passage: The taxi was booked for five the next morning. At nine at night Noor suddenly looked at the cage on the veranda where her two budgies were dozing. "Who will feed them?" Nobody had thought of it. She checked the clock, hurried next door and knocked. "Shalini Aunty, can you feed my birds for a week?" Shalini Aunty smiled. "Show me what to do." Noor wrote on a card: seed from the blue tin, fresh water, cover the cage at night. She pinned it to the cage and put her family's phone number at the bottom. Then she went to pack her own bag.

qa.q: What time was the taxi booked for?
qa.a: The taxi was booked for five the next morning.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she realised nobody had thought of the birds?
qa.a: Alarmed and anxious, since she hurried next door at once.

qa.q: What else could Noor do to make the plan safer, and why?
qa.a: Noor could show Shalini Aunty the cage and tins in person once, so the card is easy to follow.

qa.q: How might Shalini Aunty see Noor's request?
qa.a: Shalini Aunty seems glad to help, since she smiles and asks to be shown what to do.

grounding: A child thinks ahead about who will feed the pet birds during a family trip and arranges it with a neighbour and a card.
